books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs
The Jackson Presidency and Jacksonian Democracy

stimulus.text: The cartoon shows President Andrew Jackson, at left, raising a cane marked “VETO” against a many-headed serpent. The serpent's heads carry state names, and the largest head, wearing a top hat, is Nicholas Biddle, president of the Second Bank of the United States. Vice President Martin Van Buren stands at the center, and the fictional common man Jack Downing stands at right with an axe. The caption reads “GENERAL JACKSON SLAYING THE MANY HEADED MONSTER.” Lithograph by Henry R. Robinson, 1836.
stimulus.source_note: Henry R. Robinson, “General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster,” lithograph, 1836 (Library of Congress). Public domain; description verified against the Library of Congress and Smithsonian records; viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The cartoon presents Jackson's attack on the Bank as

options.text: a heroic fight against a corrupt monster

options.misconception: That is the “King Andrew” view; this print cheers Jackson on, with the common man Jack Downing at his side.

options.text: a private quarrel between Jackson and Biddle
options.misconception: The monster has heads in every state, so the fight is about a national institution, not two men.

options.text: a mistake that ruined the economy
options.misconception: The print shows Jackson winning, not failing; the Panic of 1837 came later and is not pictured here.

rationales.A: Jackson swings his “VETO” cane like a hero slaying a beast, while Van Buren and the common man Jack Downing fight beside him.
rationales.B: This print is on Jackson's side; the tyrant charge belongs to the “King Andrew” cartoon.
rationales.C: The serpent spans the states, so the fight is national, not personal.
rationales.D: The print shows a victory; the Panic of 1837 is not in the picture.
rationales.general:
1. Watch the hero's pose. Jackson raises his cane and drives at the serpent, while his allies back him.
2. Watch the monster. It is a many-headed beast, the classic shape of corruption in cartoons.
3. Compare with “King Andrew.” That print makes Jackson a tyrant; this one makes him a dragon-slayer.
Background: The Democratic press celebrated the Bank War, while Whig prints attacked Jackson as a king, so the same events drew opposite pictures.
Remember: ask whose side the cartoon is on before you read its argument.

figures.caption: General Jackson slaying the many headed monster, 1836. Jackson attacks the Bank.
